questions.q: The old Oja API paged products with ?page=2&limit=20 (SQL OFFSET 20). A partner saw a product on page 1 again on page 2. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: An offset counts rows from the start. When a new row sorts in before the ones already shown, everything shifts by one, and the last row of page 1 becomes the first row of page 2. Keyset pagination ("after id 57") is anchored to a row, not a position, so it cannot repeat.
options: The database returned rows in random order
A product was added before the rows the client had already seen, so every row moved one place and page 2 started one row earlier
The limit was too small
The client sent the request twice

questions.q: Why does the Oja API model logging in as POST /v1/tokens?
questions.explain: Thinking in resources turns the verb "log in" into a noun: a token is created. POST is not more secret than GET over HTTPS, but a password must never go into a URL, where it ends up in logs; that is a second reason to use a body.
options: Because GET requests cannot carry JSON
Logging in creates something new, an access token, and POST creates resources
Because tokens are secret and POST is encrypted
Because every route must be a POST

questions.q: Why is cancelling POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel rather than PATCH /v1/orders/{id} with {"status": "cancelled"}?
questions.explain: Cancelling is a state transition with a side effect (stock goes back). A small action resource exposes exactly that transition. A status PATCH invites {"status": "placed"} or "shipped", and every one needs a rule.
options: PATCH is not allowed to change a status
PATCH cannot have a side effect
With a generic PATCH the client could also send other statuses, so the server would have to forbid every transition but one; the action names the one allowed transition and its side effect
The OpenAPI document cannot describe PATCH

questions.q: Bola asks for GET /v1/orders/1, which is Ada's order. Why does the API answer 404 instead of 403?
questions.explain: An attacker who changes the id in the URL learns nothing: existing and missing orders look the same. The SQL WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2 finds no row in both cases, so the code does not even need a separate check.
options: Because 403 is only for admins
A 403 would confirm that order 1 exists; 404 gives the same answer as for an order that does not exist
Because the order really is deleted for Bola
Because 404 is cached by browsers

questions.q: In POST /v1/orders, "not enough stock" is 409 and "product 99 does not exist" is 422. What is the idea behind the split?
questions.explain: A client can react differently: after a 409 it can show "sold out, try later" or reduce the quantity; after a 422 it has a bug or stale data. Syntax and schema errors are 400, before any business rule runs.
options: 409 is for users, 422 for admins
422 means the JSON could not be parsed
Out of stock conflicts with the current state and may succeed later; an unknown product id is a request that will never succeed as it is
There is no difference; both could be 400

questions.q: Ada's phone sends POST /v1/orders/7/cancel, loses the response, and sends it again. The order is already cancelled. What should the second request return, and why?
questions.explain: The client wanted the order cancelled, and it is. Returning the current state makes retries safe. The conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'placed' guarantees the stock is only returned by the request that actually changed the status.
options: 409, because the order is already cancelled
404, because the order is gone
200 with the cancelled order, and no stock goes back a second time: the action is idempotent, so the retry is harmless
500, because the state machine was violated

questions.q: Which change can Oja ship in /v1 without breaking an old mobile app that nobody updated?
questions.explain: Additive changes keep old clients working, because they ignore fields they do not know. Renames, type changes and removals break them and need /v2. This is also why responses allow additional properties in the OpenAPI document.
options: Renaming priceKobo to price
Changing priceKobo from integer kobo to a naira string
Adding a new optional field imageUrl to products
Removing GET /v1/orders

questions.q: Why does order_lines store its own price_kobo instead of joining to products.price_kobo when showing an order?
questions.explain: The product's price is current data; the order line's price is a historical fact. Copying it at the moment of sale is the correct model, not a denormalisation shortcut.
options: To save disk space
Because foreign keys cannot point at prices
An order must keep the price it was sold at; tomorrow's price change must not rewrite yesterday's receipt
Because the join would be slow

questions.q: A teammate replaces the UNIQUE constraint on users.email with code: "SELECT the e-mail; if no row, INSERT". Tests still pass. What breaks?
questions.explain: There is a gap between the read and the write. Only the database can close it: a UNIQUE constraint, used with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, makes one insert win and turns the other into a clean 409.
options: Nothing; the code does the same check
Two registrations at the same moment can both see "no row" and both insert, creating two accounts with one e-mail
Registration becomes slower but stays correct
Logins stop working

questions.q: Oja's requireUser reads the user's role from the database on every request instead of trusting a roles claim in the JWT. What does that buy?
questions.explain: A claim in a token is fixed until the token expires. Reading the role fresh makes changes take effect at once. Revoking the token itself before it expires needs sessions, which the next lesson adds.
options: Tokens become shorter and faster to verify
A demoted admin loses admin rights on the next request, and tokens of deleted accounts stop working, at the cost of one primary-key lookup
The token no longer needs a signature
Nothing; the token's claims are already checked

questions.q: Why does login run verifyPassword against a decoy hash when the e-mail is unknown?
questions.explain: Password hashing is deliberately slow. Skipping it for unknown e-mails makes those answers measurably faster, which leaks exactly what the identical error message was meant to hide.
options: To create the account automatically
To warm up the password hasher
So "unknown e-mail" takes as long as "wrong password"; otherwise the response time tells an attacker which e-mails have accounts
Because verifyPassword throws without a hash

questions.q: Why does Oja's error handler build the body from error.code and error.message instead of sending serializePublicError(error)?
questions.explain: The lesson's example put a warehouse name and a supplier cost into a DomainError's metadata; serializePublicError passed them on. Building the body from named fields is an allow-list for errors, just like output schemas are for data.
options: serializePublicError does not exist in @zudojs/errors
serializePublicError includes the stack trace
For an error that may be shown to clients, serializePublicError includes the whole metadata, and metadata is written for logs, not for clients
serializePublicError changes the status code

questions.q: Why does products.list ask the database for limit + 1 rows?
questions.explain: The extra row is only looked at, never returned. count(*) on every page request gets slower as the table grows; one extra row costs nothing.
options: Because SQL LIMIT is off by one
If the extra row exists, there is a next page; this avoids counting the whole table
To return one bonus product
To make the cursor signature longer

questions.q: What does signing the cursor with cursorSecret protect against?
questions.explain: A signature proves integrity, not secrecy: the payload is plain base64url JSON anyone can read. A changed payload with an old signature is rejected with 400, and allowedFields rejects unexpected keys.
options: Someone reading the cursor's contents
A client editing the cursor, for example to jump to arbitrary positions or smuggle other fields into the query
The cursor expiring
SQL injection through the category filter

questions.q: The contract test did not report an extra cost_kobo field in a product response. Why, and what protects against that leak instead?
questions.explain: Response schemas are deliberately open to additions. A contract test catches wrong types, missing fields and undocumented statuses. Leaks are stopped where data leaves the database: named columns, never SELECT *, and allow-list parsing.
options: Ajv ignores numbers
The contract test only checks status codes
The document allows additional properties so fields can be added without breaking clients; the protection is SQL that names its columns and output schemas like UserOut
cost_kobo is part of the Product schema

questions.q: Why does createRouter get a notFoundHandler and a methodNotAllowedHandler?
questions.explain: One error envelope means one error-handling path in every client. The router's own answers must be brought into line too. The 405 also sets the Allow header.
options: Without them the router crashes on unknown paths
The router's default 404 and 405 bodies have a different shape, so a mistyped URL would be the one error clients cannot parse like the others
They add authentication to unknown routes
They are required by mountOpenAPI

questions.q: A request fails because the database is down. What should the client receive?
questions.explain: Internal details help attackers and confuse users. The request id connects the customer's report to the log line that holds the real cause.
options: The database error message, so the developer can fix it
The stack trace, but only in production
A generic message and a request id; the real cause goes to the log with the same id
An empty 200 response
A 404, because the data was not found

questions.q: The test suite runs on PGlite. Which kind of bug can it miss that a real PostgreSQL server with a connection pool would expose?
questions.explain: PGlite is real PostgreSQL, so SQL and constraints behave the same. But with a single connection, two "simultaneous" orders run one after the other, which hides races. Run the concurrency tests against a real server in CI.
options: Wrong SQL syntax
A missing CHECK constraint
Races between concurrent transactions, because PGlite runs one transaction at a time
Wrong status codes

questions.q: A phone sends POST /v1/orders, the connection drops before the response, and the app retries. What happens with this lesson's API, and what fixes it?
questions.explain: A transaction makes one order all-or-nothing; it cannot know that two requests are the same intent. Only a key chosen by the client, once per intent, can. The payments use case builds this.
options: Nothing bad: the transaction prevents duplicates
The second request gets 409 automatically
Two orders are placed; the fix is an Idempotency-Key header whose stored response is replayed for the retry
The second request gets 404

questions.q: listMine loads 50 order ids, then calls load for each (two queries each). How many queries is that, and what is the pattern called?
questions.explain: One query for the ids plus two per order. The fix is to fetch all orders and then all their lines with WHERE order_id = ANY($1) in two queries, and group them in code.
options: 3 queries; eager loading
50 queries; batching
101 queries; the N+1 query problem
1 query; a join

questions.q: Why does ProductQuery cap limit at 50?
questions.explain: Every input that controls work needs an upper bound. The cap also appears in the OpenAPI document, so clients know it before they hit the 400.
options: JSON cannot hold more than 50 items
Without a cap, one request with limit=1000000 makes the server read and serialize the whole table
OpenAPI requires a maximum
PostgreSQL limits LIMIT to 50

questions.q: ProductPatch is NewProduct.omit(["sku"]).partial().strict(). An admin sends {"sku": "new-sku", "stock": 5}. What happens?
questions.explain: Stripping would hide the admin's mistake: they would believe the SKU changed. .strict() turns an unknown field into a clear error. For responses, stripping is right; for update requests, strictness is kinder.
options: The stock changes and the sku is silently ignored
Both fields change
400: .strict() reports the unknown key sku, and nothing changes
500, because sku is unique

questions.q: currentUser(ctx) throws "requireUser is missing on this route" when no user is in the state. Why not return undefined and let the route decide?
questions.explain: Security code should fail closed. A missing check that silently passes is the classic way an admin route becomes public.
options: Because TypeScript does not allow undefined
A forgotten requireUser then fails loudly (a 500 and a log line in tests) instead of quietly treating the caller as allowed
Because the route would get a 401
For performance

questions.q: An order has three lines. Lines 1 and 2 take their stock, line 3 finds too little. With withTransaction, what is the final state?
questions.explain: The error leaves the callback, so withTransaction rolls back everything done inside it. The client gets 409 and the stock is exactly as before, which the "rolls back every line" test checks.
options: Lines 1 and 2 keep their stock change; the order is saved with two lines
Lines 1 and 2 keep their stock change; no order is saved
Nothing changed: the ConflictError rolls back lines 1 and 2, and no order exists
The order is saved as "failed"

questions.explain: schema.coerce.number() turns the query string "5" into the number 5. The unknown key page is stripped, and the missing limit gets its default of 20. Missing optional keys are simply absent, and the result follows the order of the schema's keys, not the input's.
options:
{ limit: 5 }
{ limit: 20, category: 'drinks' }

{ limit: '5' }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The e-mail is trimmed and lower-cased before the format check, the name is trimmed, and role is not in the schema, so it is dropped. The server alone decides roles.
options: { email: 'bola@example.com', name: 'Bola' }
{ email: 'bola@example.com', name: 'Bola', role: 'admin' }
{ email: '  Bola@Example.COM ', name: ' Bola ' }
{ email: 'Bola@Example.COM', name: 'Bola' }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: omit removed sku from the shape, partial made the rest optional (so a missing priceKobo is fine), and strict turns the unknown sku into an issue instead of stripping it.
options:
true
{ stock: 4 }

true
{ stock: 4, sku: 'rice-5kg' }

questions.q: Keyset pagination over an array. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each page starts after the last id seen, so the new row with id 0 (which sorts first) cannot shift anything. The last page has no extra row, so next is null.
options: { ids: [ 1, 2 ], next: 2 } { ids: [ 4, 7 ], next: 7 } { ids: [ 9 ], next: null }
{ ids: [ 1, 2 ], next: 2 } { ids: [ 2, 4 ], next: 4 } { ids: [ 7, 9 ], next: null }
{ ids: [ 1, 2 ], next: 2 } { ids: [ 0, 4 ], next: 4 } { ids: [ 7, 9 ], next: null }
{ ids: [ 1, 2 ], next: 2 } { ids: [ 4, 7 ], next: 7 } { ids: [ 9 ], next: 9 }

questions.q: The same catalogue with offset pagination. What does this print?
questions.explain: Page 2 means "skip 2". After acha was inserted at the front, skipping 2 lands on garri again: the client sees it twice and never sees yam on this page. This is partner complaint 1.
options: [ 'beans', 'garri' ] [ 'garri', 'rice' ]
[ 'beans', 'garri' ] [ 'rice', 'yam' ]
[ 'acha', 'beans' ] [ 'garri', 'rice' ]
[ 'beans', 'garri' ] [ 'acha', 'rice' ]

questions.explain: ConflictError is 409 and DomainError is 422, both exposed, so their own code and message go out. A TypeError is a bug: it is normalized to a 500 that is not exposed, and the client sees only the generic body.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For an exposed error, serializePublicError passes the metadata on. Here that would tell a stranger who owns order 7. That is why Oja's handler builds the body from code and message only.
options: 404 { orderId: 7, ownerId: 42 }
404 undefined
500 undefined

questions.q: An idempotent cancel over plain objects. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only the call that changes the status from placed returns the stock. Later calls find the order cancelled and just report its state, which is what makes retries safe.
options: cancelled cancelled cancelled 3
cancelled cancelled cancelled 7
cancelled placed cancelled 5
cancelled undefined undefined 3

questions.q: Route parameters are strings. What does this print?
questions.explain: Coercion turns "12" into 12; then the number rules run. A non-number, zero or a fraction never reaches the database, so /v1/orders/abc is a 400 instead of a 500 from PostgreSQL.
options:
12 12
0 Expected >= 1, received 0
abc Cannot coerce string to number
1.5 Expected integer, received 1.5

12 '12'

abc Cannot coerce string to number
1.5 1.5

12 12

questions.q: Totals in integer kobo. What does this print?
questions.explain: Integer kobo add up exactly: 2 500 000 + 200 000 + 5 997 = 2 705 997. Only when displaying do you split into naira and kobo. Floating-point naira could produce long fractions.

questions.q: Write nextPage(products, afterId, limit) for products sorted by id. It returns { data, nextAfter }: at most limit products with an id greater than afterId, and the id to continue after, or null when there is no further product. Page through the list with limit 2 and print each page's ids.
questions.explain: Fetching one extra row tells you whether another page exists without counting. The last page has no extra row, so nextAfter is null and the loop stops.

questions.q: Write errorBody(problem) that turns an internal problem into Oja's envelope. problem is { status, code, message, issues? }. For status 500 and above, the body is { error: { code: "INTERNAL", message: "Something went wrong on our side", requestId } } with the given requestId; otherwise { error: { code, message } }, plus issues only when there are any. Print the three examples as JSON.
questions.explain: One function decides every error body, so clients need one parser. The 500 body never repeats the internal message; the request id links it to the log.

questions.q: Write placeOrder(stock, items) over a Map of SKU to quantity. Either every line is taken, or nothing changes and it throws new Error("Not enough stock for <sku>"). Also reject an order that lists the same SKU twice with "List each product once". Print the results of the three orders and the final stock.
questions.explain: Checking every line before changing anything gives all-or-nothing in memory. In the database, a transaction gives the same guarantee even though each line changes stock as it goes. The duplicate check matters there too: two lines for one product would otherwise hit the order_lines primary key.
questions.expected:
Not enough stock for rice
List each product once
placed
[ [ 'rice', 1 ], [ 'zobo', 6 ] ]

questions.q: With @zudojs/schema, write a UserOut schema with id (integer), email, name and role ("customer" or "admin"), and use it to turn the database row below into a safe response. Print the result.
questions.explain: An object schema strips keys it does not list, so the hash and the internal counter never leave the server, including columns someone adds next year.
questions.starter:
import { schema } from "@zudojs/schema";

const row = { id: 4, email: "bola@example.com", name: "Bola", role: "customer", password_hash: "scrypt$16384$...", failed_logins: 2 };

questions.q: Write statusFor(situation) that returns the status Oja's API uses for each situation name below, following the lesson's design table. Print each situation with its status.
questions.explain: Each status tells the client what to do next: fix the request (400, 422), sign in (401), stop (403), treat it as missing (404), retry later or change the request (409). Cancelling again is a success because the action is idempotent.
questions.expected:
created: 201
invalid body: 400
no token: 401
customer on admin route: 403
someone else's order: 404
email taken: 409
out of stock: 409
unknown product: 422
cancel again: 200

questions.q: Orders live in an array. Write findOrder(orders, userId, orderId) that returns the order only if it belongs to userId, and otherwise { status: 404 }, the same answer whether the order is someone else's or does not exist. Print the three lookups.
questions.explain: Put the owner into the lookup itself, like WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2. Then there is no second step that could be forgotten, and a stranger cannot tell "not yours" from "does not exist".

questions.q: Write formatNaira(kobo) that formats integer kobo as naira with thousands separators and exactly two decimals, without floating-point division errors, e.g. 2705997 becomes ₦27,059.97. Print it for 2705997, 50000 and 5.
questions.explain: Keep money as integers everywhere and only split into naira and kobo for display. The API itself sends priceKobo as an integer and leaves display to the client, which is what the document promises.

questions.q: With @zudojs/schema, write ProductQuery: an optional category from "grains", "drinks", "spices", and a limit that is coerced from a string, is an integer from 1 to 50, and defaults to 20. Print the result of safeParse for the three query objects: success and either the data or the first issue's path.
questions.explain: Query strings are always strings, so the schema coerces, checks the range and fills the default. The same schema generates the OpenAPI parameters, so the documented limits are the enforced ones.
questions.starter:
import { schema } from "@zudojs/schema";

const queries = [{ limit: "10", category: "spices" }, {}, { limit: "500" }];
